title: Azure monitoring strategy: logs, metrics and traces
description: Design an observability strategy in Azure using logs, metrics, and distributed traces. Learn how to collect signals, route them to the right services, and avoid common monitoring gaps.

data.text: Production incidents are inevitable. What separates a painful outage from a quick recovery is observability. Azure provides three core signal types: logs (discrete events), metrics (time-series numbers), and traces (distributed request paths). A solid monitoring strategy uses all three.

Logs tell you what happened. A log entry might say 'order checkout failed with 500' or 'database connection pool exhausted.' Metrics tell you how much or how fast. CPU percentage, request count, and queue depth are all metrics. Traces tell you where time was spent across services. In a microservices architecture, a single request may touch five or ten services; distributed tracing stitches those hops together.

terms.definition: Discrete, timestamped records of events, usually structured as JSON in Azure Monitor.
Numerical measurements collected at regular intervals, such as CPU percentage or request latency.
End-to-end records of a request as it moves through distributed services, showing latency per hop.

data.text: Azure Monitor is the backbone of Azure observability. It ingests logs from almost every Azure resource, stores them in a Log Analytics workspace, and lets you query with Kusto Query Language (KQL). Metrics are stored separately in the Azure Monitor Metrics database, which is optimized for fast aggregation and charting.

data.title: KQL query for failed requests
data.content: Run this in Log Analytics to see the last hour of failed requests from an App Service.
data.code:
requests
| where timestamp > ago(1h)
| where success == false
| summarize count() by resultCode, bin(timestamp, 5m)
| order by timestamp desc

data.text: Application Insights automatically collects dependency calls, exceptions, and request telemetry. When you enable distributed tracing, it generates a traceId that links all operations for a single request across services. You can visualize the end-to-end path in the Application Insights portal and spot the slowest hop.

data.title: Sampling matters
data.text: High-traffic applications should use adaptive sampling in Application Insights. Without sampling, telemetry volume and cost can grow faster than your traffic. Aim for 5-20% sampling in production, with exceptions kept at 100%.

The goal of monitoring is action, not dashboards. Every alert should map to a runbook or an automatic response. In Azure Monitor, use metric alerts for fast numerical thresholds, log alerts for complex conditions, and smart detection rules for Application Insights to catch anomalies without manual thresholds.

data.title: Monitoring checklist
items: Route all Azure resource logs to a central Log Analytics workspace.
Enable Application Insights for every application tier.
Set up metric alerts for availability, latency, and error rate.
Create log alerts for specific error conditions, such as repeated 500s.
Use action groups to notify the right team via email, SMS, or webhook.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Logs answer 'what,' metrics answer 'how much,' and traces answer 'where.'
Azure Monitor unifies logs and metrics; Application Insights adds distributed traces.
Alert on user impact, not just infrastructure noise.
Sampling controls telemetry cost without losing diagnostic value.
data.takeaway: A monitoring strategy is complete when you can detect, diagnose, and resolve an incident using only Azure signals.
